title: From Pixels, Without Pre-training:Joint Generative and Self-Supervised Representation Learning in One Model

paper.title:
From Pixels, Without Pre-training: Joint Generative and
Self-Supervised Representation Learning in One Model
paper.abstract:
Abstract Strong image generation models today are conditioned on class labels, aligned to frozen pretrained encoders, or built on separately trained autoencoders or tokenizers. While effective, the cost is that generation becomes contingent on supervision and pretraining: labels must be annotated, and encoders, autoencoders, and tokenizers must be pretrained for the target domain. This paper studies joint generative and self-supervised representation learning in one model , such that generation is self-conditioned without any labels or pretrained models. This is challenging since the two objectives are mismatched: contrastive learning consumes clean augmented views and keeps coarse, invariant semantics, while flow matching consumes noisy images and must preserve the fine detail and spatial layout that contrastive learning discards. We propose a framework Self-conditioned Generation on Self-supervised representation (SCION), whose core is a single pixel-space encoder conditioned on both the diffusion timestep and a conditioning embedding. The encoder serves two roles that differ in what that embedding is. For representation learning, the conditioning embedding is one learned global vector shared by all images, and the encoder’s [CLS] token yields the semantic embedding trained by the contrastive loss. For generative training, the conditioning embedding is the [CLS] embedding of the image itself, and the encoder’s patch tokens pass through a decoder to predict the image. To sample without a reference image at inference, we also learn a prior over the embedding in the same run. With gradient-norm balancing and stop-gradient tricks, all losses are jointly optimized in a single run. The resulting method is fully self-supervised, with no pretrained model and no labels.
On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , with the same JiT-B/16 recipe and without representation guidance, SCION reaches 8.92 8.92 FID,
surpassing the class-unconditional baselines iREPA, which aligns to a pretrained DINOv2 ( 46.44 46.44 ), and RCG, which conditions on it ( 14.27 14.27 ).
Under the JiT-L/16 recipe, SCION achieves the best pixel-space class-unconditional FID of 5.89 5.89 and 3.47 3.47 without and with representation guidance, outperforming RCG with the ADM recipe ( 6.24 6.24 ).

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in image generation ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Yet many strong systems rely on class labels for semantic conditioning ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Li and He, 2026 ) , frozen pretrained encoders for conditioning or representation alignment ( Li et al., 2024a ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) , or separately trained autoencoders for latent-space generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . These dependencies add annotation or pretraining costs and complicate extension to domains where suitable labels or pretrained models are unavailable. A central challenge is therefore to enable semantically self-conditioned generation , where the semantic representations that condition generation are learned within the diffusion model itself, jointly with the generative process. We pursue semantic self-conditioned generation under four “S” requirements: self-contained , without pretrained components, including autoencoders and tokenizers; self-supervised , without label supervision anywhere in the pipeline, including that inherited through pretrained components; single-model , with representations produced by the generator’s own network; and single-stage , with all components learned jointly from scratch. Existing methods (cf. Table 1 ) address different aspects of this goal but satisfy these requirements only partially ( Li and He, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2023 ; Preechakul et al., 2022 ; Hudson et al., 2024 ; Wang and He, 2025 ) . These comparisons highlight the remaining challenge: achieving semantic self-conditioning under all four “S” requirements, with useful representations and unconditional synthesis learned together within one model. Figure 1 : Generation and Representation capabilities of different models trained on ImageNet 256 × 256 256{\times}256 with 400 400 epochs. FID under the ADM evaluation protocol. A segment joins a method’s class-conditional and class-unconditional variants, so its length is what the class label buys. A natural approach to semantically self-conditioned generation is to learn the conditioning representations through contrastive self-supervised learning, which extracts semantics directly from unlabeled images ( Chen et al., 2020a ; He et al., 2020 ; Yuan et al., 2022 ) . However, integrating self-supervised representation learning with flow matching in one network requires reconciling their conflicting input and output requirements. Contrastive learning operates on clean augmented views and encourages compact semantic embeddings that suppress variations in appearance and spatial layout. Flow matching instead operates on noisy images and requires dense predictions that recover fine visual detail and spatial structure. The shared network must therefore accommodate both clean and noisy inputs while supporting semantic invariance without discarding information needed for synthesis. Joint training further couples the generator to an evolving conditioning representation, and sampling requires obtaining conditioning embeddings without a reference image. To address these challenges, we propose S elf- C onditioned Generation on Self-Supervised Representat ion (SCION), a framework for semantically self-conditioned generation through joint generative and self-supervised representation learning. At its core is a single pixel-space transformer encoder conditioned on both a timestep and a conditioning embedding. Our key idea is to use this encoder in two conditioning modes with different readouts. For representation learning, the encoder processes clean augmented views using a learned global conditioning vector shared across all images, and a contrastive objective trains its [CLS] embedding. For generative learning, the same encoder processes noisy images conditioned on the clean image’s own [CLS] embedding, and a decoder maps its patch tokens to a clean-image prediction under a flow matching objective. This design keeps contrastive inputs clean while using spatial features for generation, allowing both objectives to train the shared encoder. To coordinate joint optimization, we employ gradient-norm balancing and stop-gradient operations. We also train a prior over the learned embeddings in the same run, enabling generation without reference images. Randomly withholding the conditioning embedding during training also supports classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) , with guidance supplied by learned representations rather than class labels. All components are trained jointly from scratch, without labels, pretrained teachers, latent autoencoders, or tokenizers. We evaluate on ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 against flow-based baselines matched on the JiT-B/16 recipe. SCION reaches 8.92 8.92 FID, improving by 6.1 × 6.1\times over the strongest self-contained baseline ( 54.14 54.14 ), and outperforming methods that import pretrained semantics, either aligning with them (iREPA, 46.44 46.44 ) or conditioning on them (RCG at matched training budget, 14.27 14.27 ). Self-representation guidance further reduces SCION to 4.20 4.20 FID, outperforming representation-guided RCG ( 5.01 5.01 ) without importing a pretrained encoder. At larger scale, SCION (JiT-L/16) reaches 5.89 5.89 unguided FID, improving on the 6.24 6.24 reported by pixel-space RCG with an ADM training recipe. sections.text: In this section, we present the proposed framework SCION, including the model structure and the training objective and strategies.

sections.heading: 3.1 The Unified Model
sections.text: Since we model images directly in pixel space, we adopt the “Just Image Transformer” (JiT) architecture for image generation ( Li and He, 2026 ) . To integrate generation with representation learning, we partition JiT into two components: an encoder f θ f_{\theta} and a decoder g ϕ g_{\phi} , parameterized by θ \theta and ϕ \phi , respectively. Both f θ f_{\theta} and g ϕ g_{\phi} consist of multiple Transformer blocks. To process an image, we split it into non-overlapping patches, linearly embed the patches into a sequence of T T tokens, and prepend a learnable [CLS] token. One encoder, two purposes. The encoder processes two types of inputs for two distinct purposes. For flow matching, it encodes a noise-diffused image 𝒙 ~ t = t ​ 𝒙 + ( 1 − t ) ​ ϵ \widetilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}=t{\bm{x}}+(1-t){\bm{\epsilon}} . For contrastive learning, it encodes a strongly augmented, non-diffused image A ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) A({\bm{x}}) . To accommodate both types of inputs, we condition the encoder f θ f_{\theta} on the timestep t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , where t = 1 t=1 corresponds to a non-diffused image. To enable semantically self-conditioned generation, we additionally condition the encoder on an embedding vector 𝒄 {\bm{c}} , whose construction is described below. We therefore write the encoder as f θ ​ ( 𝒛 ∣ t , 𝒄 ) f_{\theta}({\bm{z}}\mid t,{\bm{c}}) , where 𝒛 {\bm{z}} denotes either a clean image 𝒙 {\bm{x}} , its augmented image A ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) A({\bm{x}}) or a noise-diffused image 𝒙 ~ t \widetilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} . The encoder output also serves two different purposes. For contrastive learning, it should provide a compact semantic representation that is invariant to variations in appearance and spatial layout. For generation, it must preserve fine-grained visual details and spatial structure. To accommodate these different requirements within a single encoder, we use two readouts from its output: the [CLS] token embedding 𝒆 ∈ ℝ d {\bm{e}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} used for representation learning, and the patch-token embeddings 𝒉 ∈ ℝ T × d {\bm{h}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} used for generation. sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: This section evaluates SCION in three settings. We first conduct a controlled comparison with baselines that share the same backbone, training budget, and flow-matching recipe, isolating the contribution of the proposed framework. We then compare with published unconditional pixel-space systems using their reported scores, providing a system-level reference. Finally, we ablate SCION to identify the contribution of each component and compare its representation with that of a contrastive-only model. Baselines . We compare SCION with vanilla flow matching (FM) and four methods built on it: Dispersive Loss ( Wang and He, 2025 ) , REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , iREPA ( Singh et al., 2026 ) , and RCG ( Li et al., 2024a ) . Thus, the baselines span FM alone, self-contained feature regularization (Dispersive), external-feature alignment (REPA/iREPA), and external semantic conditioning (RCG). Setup . All controlled methods use the same JiT-B/16 backbone ( Li and He, 2026 ) with attention residuals (Appendix F ), flow matching recipe, ImageNet-1K ( 256 × 256 256\times 256 ) training data ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) , and a total training budget of 400 400 epochs. The baselines that import semantics use a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , pretrained on external data. REPA and iREPA retain their original split of 4 4 encoder and 8 8 decoder blocks, whereas Dispersive Loss and SCION use 8 8 encoder and 4 4 decoder blocks. We split RCG’s training budget between its generator and prior, training for 200 200 epochs each. We also evaluate RCG with both its original prior architecture and ours: the original architecture performs better, so we report that result. Evaluation . We evaluate generation with FID and Inception Score (IS) under the ADM protocol ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) on 50 50 K samples. We evaluate representations using ImageNet top-1 accuracy ( Acc. ) and the average accuracy across eight datasets for transfer learning ( transfer-8 ; datasets listed in Appendix E.2 ). For both probes, we train a logistic-regression classifier on the frozen representations produced by the model. For the baselines, the representation is the mean pooling of patch token embeddings at the encoder–decoder split, or after the last block for vanilla JiT and RCG; for SCION, we use its [CLS] token at its own split. Training and evaluation details are in Appendix E , and architecture details in Appendix F .

sections.text: To isolate the contribution of each component, we use the same JiT-B/16 recipe as the controlled comparison and train every model for 200 200 epochs. From flow matching to SCION. We decompose SCION by sequentially adding its components to unconditional flow matching. Table 5 shows that contrastive learning first makes the representation useful, increasing Acc. from 10.65 % 10.65\% to 65.43 % 65.43\% and transfer-8 from 26.19 % 26.19\% to 76.69 % 76.69\% , while slightly improving FID from 61.17 61.17 to 57.40 57.40 . Gradient-norm balancing further reduces FID to 54.79 54.79 while maintaining representation quality and avoiding manual selection of the contrastive weight. Adding representation self-conditioning with the jointly learned prior converts these representation gains into substantially better generation, reducing FID to 11.66 11.66 . Finally, CBC completes SCION and reaches 10.10 10.10 FID, with 71.32 % 71.32\% Acc. and 79.73 % 79.73\% transfer-8. Appendix C.1 provides a more detailed ladder. Comparison with contrastive-only training. Table 5 also compares with a contrastive-only control using the same 8 8 -layer encoder, evaluated at 200 200 epochs. Its learning rate, temperature, and weight decay are tuned independently for contrastive learning. SCION reaches 71.32 % 71.32\% Acc., close to the control’s 71.76 % 71.76\% , while attaining higher transfer-8 accuracy ( 79.73 % 79.73\% versus 77.68 % 77.68\% ). Thus, joint training retains representation quality comparable to dedicated contrastive learning while also learning to generate. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented SCION, a framework that jointly learns image generation and semantic representations in a single pixel-space model, trained from scratch without labels or pretrained components. By integrating contrastive learning with flow matching, representation self-conditioning, and a jointly learned embedding prior, SCION supports both representation extraction and unconditional image generation. Experiments on ImageNet demonstrate substantial improvements over matched generative baselines while retaining representation quality competitive with dedicated contrastive learning. These results show that strong generation and useful representations can be learned together in a self-contained, self-supervised training process. Future work will explore downstream applications and extensions to domains where labels and pretrained models are scarce.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Like other image-generation methods, SCION could be used to produce misleading or harmful imagery. We consider the potential for misuse of the models studied here to be limited by their current image fidelity, 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, and class-unconditional sampling without text-based or explicit identity control. These limitations do not eliminate risk: generated images and learned representations may reflect biases or sensitive content in the training data, and we have not evaluated training-image memorization or demographic fairness. By removing the need for labels and pretrained components, the method also lowers the barrier to training on new domains and could enable more capable models. Such extensions would require assessment of risks appropriate to their capabilities and intended use. Training uses multiple NVIDIA H200 GPUs (Appendix E ), with an associated energy cost. Our single-stage approach avoids separate pretraining of encoders, autoencoders, or tokenizers, although we do not establish a reduction in total compute or energy consumption relative to other approaches.

Conditional GANs established that class information can substantially improve image synthesis ( Mirza and Osindero, 2014 ; Brock et al., 2019 ) . Thus, although DDPM initially demonstrated high-quality unconditional synthesis ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , it was soon followed by Improved DDPM incorporating class labels into diffusion ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) . Classifier guidance further strengthened the effect of this semantic signal ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , while classifier-free guidance subsequently removed the need for a separate classifier, retaining label conditioning ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . Together, these developments made semantics a central lever for generation, but supplied them directly through annotations. Alongside this use of labels, efforts to reduce computation brought another source of semantics into the pipeline. Latent diffusion and flow models generate through pretrained autoencoders ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Dao et al., 2023 ) , a setting later continued by transformer generators such as DiT and SiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Ma et al., 2024 ) . Although introduced for compression, these autoencoders can inherit semantic information from their training objectives. VQGAN ( Esser et al., 2021 ) , for example, uses a perceptual loss ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) based on supervised features ( Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014 ) . The semantic information carried by these tokenizers can therefore shape the representations learned on top of them ( Chen et al., 2025b ) and also benefit generation beyond reconstruction fidelity ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Importing representations for generation. Beyond the semantics inherited from autoencoders, generators can also draw on representations supplied explicitly by pretrained encoders. Some align autoencoder latents with frozen features ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) , while representation autoencoders generate directly in a pretrained encoder’s latent space ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Others bring the same semantic signal into the generator itself through feature alignment, as in REPA and iREPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) . Since fixed alignment can conflict with generative detail, subsequent work refines how pretrained features interact with generative training ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . ReDi instead models images and pretrained features jointly ( Kouzelis et al., 2025 ) . Beyond defining the latent space or guiding internal features, representations can serve directly as conditions. RCG and DLC take this route, conditioning on pretrained embeddings or discrete codes derived from them, and training separate models to sample them ( Li et al., 2024a ; Lavoie et al., 2025 ) . Related retrieval and instance-conditioned methods obtain conditions from real images ( Blattmann et al., 2022 ; Bordes et al., 2022 ; Casanova et al., 2021 ) , while earlier approaches replace labels with clusters or proxy labels ( Lucic et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2020 ; Bao et al., 2022a ; Hu et al., 2023 ) . These approaches show that semantic conditioning need not rely on class labels, but importing representations introduces dependencies on pretrained components or separate training stages. Learning these representations within the generator itself would therefore reduce the pipeline’s external dependencies. Self-contained generation. The pretrained components used by many of these approaches motivate a complementary direction that removes such dependencies. Pixel-space diffusion and flow models avoid the upstream autoencoder ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) , and recent recipes have made this setting increasingly competitive at high resolution ( Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Li and He, 2026 ) . Operating on pixels therefore removes one dependency, although it does not itself replace the semantic signal supplied by class labels. Dispersive Loss and Repulsor extend this effort to representation regularization, pushing apart intermediate features without a pretrained representation encoder ( Wang and He, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . In particular, Dispersive Loss finds positive-pair regularization sensitive to noisy-view construction and therefore retains only contrastive repulsion, arguing that denoising supplies attraction. The features nevertheless remain auxiliary regularizers, without downstream representation evaluation or explicit semantic conditioning, and the high-quality ImageNet settings retain class labels. Joint generation and representation learning. Self-supervised learning offers a source of such semantics through pretext tasks ( Noroozi and Favaro, 2016 ; Gidaris et al., 2018 ) , masked modeling ( Bao et al., 2022b ; He et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2021 ) , self-distillation ( Grill et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2021 ) , and contrastive objectives ( van den Oord et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2020a ; He et al., 2020 ) . The latter learn invariances by matching augmented views of the same image while separating different images. Although SimCLR benefits from large batches ( Chen et al., 2020b ) , SogCLR reduces this requirement through a moving-average approximation to a global contrastive objective ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) . These objectives provide useful representations, but on their own do not define an image generator. Joint methods therefore seek to combine the two capabilities. MAGE learns and evaluates both in one transformer ( Li et al., 2023 ) , but operates on pretrained VQGAN tokens ( Esser et al., 2021 ) , thus retaining the inherited perceptual supervision discussed above. ADDP and LZN follow a similar joint learning goal through tokenized or modular latent pipelines ( Tian et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . A different route makes the learned representation a condition for a diffusion decoder. DiffAE learns this code through reconstruction, then fits a latent prior for unconditional sampling ( Preechakul et al., 2022 ) . InfoDiffusion likewise conditions diffusion on learned codes, sampled from a prior or a separately trained prior model ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . SODA moves from reconstruction to cross-view generation, using a source view’s code to generate a related view ( Hudson et al., 2024 ) . All three methods produce their representations with an encoder separate from the diffusion decoder, and SODA additionally requires a source image for synthesis. SCION follows the joint learning goal while bringing the representation into the pixel-space generator itself, where it is learned, evaluated, and used to condition synthesis. A prior trained in the same run supplies conditions without a source image, combining the four requirements summarized in Table 6 and defined in Section 1 .

sections.heading: C.4 Analysis of the representation prior
sections.text: At inference, the generator is conditioned on a representation sampled from the prior e ω e_{\omega} , so sample quality depends on both the generator and the prior. To separate the two, we replace the prior sample with the representation 𝒆 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) {\bm{e}}({\bm{x}}) of a real training image, which we call oracle conditioning. It requires real images at generation time, so it serves as a diagnostic rather than as a way to sample.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: All results use SCION (B/16) at 400 400 epochs, without guidance. We draw a conditioning set of 50 50 images per class, 50 50 K in total, from the ImageNet training set with a fixed seed, and generate one image from the representation of each. The prior arm consists of 50 50 K images generated by the same model from prior samples, namely the samples behind the 8.92 8.92 FID in Table 3 . We compute precision and recall (Appendix E.2 ) of both arms against two references: the conditioning set itself, and a disjoint set drawn in the same way from the remaining training images. For each reference we use a random 10 10 K subset for precision and recall computation, matching what ADM does.

sections.heading: Real representations raise recall, prior samples raise precision.
sections.text: Table 11 reports the results. The prior arm serves as a control: its samples were generated from neither reference, and it scores nearly the same against both, with precision .718 .718 and .722 .722 and recall .524 .524 and .510 .510 . The two references therefore behave alike for samples not generated from either, so a gap between them in the oracle arm reflects that its samples were generated from the conditioning images. The oracle arm shows such a gap. Its recall is .828 .828 against the conditioning set and .664 .664 against the disjoint set, so the generated images cover the specific images they were conditioned on better than other images from the same distribution. The representation thus carries image-specific content into the generated image. Against the disjoint set, where the oracle arm has no such advantage, it still reaches higher recall than the prior arm, .664 .664 against .510 .510 , at lower precision, .626 .626 against .722 .722 . The two arms share the generator and differ only in the conditioning vectors, so this difference is due to the prior: conditioned on real representations, the samples cover more of the reference images, while conditioned on prior samples, a larger fraction of them falls inside the reference manifold. sections.text: This appendix gives the training and evaluation setup behind Section 4 . Table 12 summarizes the main hyperparameters at both scales. Unless an experiment states otherwise, the settings below are the defaults for every ImageNet-1K ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) run. All experiments are run on nodes of 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. To speed up experiments, we train on up to 3 nodes for B/16 and 6 nodes for L/16.

sections.heading: E.1 Training setup
sections.text: We follow JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) for the generative hyperparameters and for ℒ CFM {\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{CFM}} , including the optimizer, the augmentation policy of the original image and the flow matching loss. We depart from it in two places, both chosen once and applied to every image generator in the comparison, baselines included: the base learning rate, which is tuned to 1 ⋅ 10 − 4 1\cdot 10^{-4} ; and the attention residuals of Appendix F . Since every arm trains at a global batch of 1024 1024 , the learning rate is 4 ⋅ 10 − 4 4\cdot 10^{-4} . For the contrastive hyperparameters and the augmentation policy of the augmented images we follow SogCLR ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) . The RCG baseline is our own re-implementation on this backbone and conditions on DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) embeddings. For its prior, we use the architecture of their official implementation 1 1 1 https://github.com/LTH14/rcg , a residual MLP with 12 12 blocks of width 1536 1536 , trained for 200 200 epochs with our flow-matching objective and prior timestep schedule. For a fair comparison, we also ran RCG with our prior, which performed worse.

sections.heading: Augmentations.
sections.text: We use k O = 1 k_{O}=1 original image and k A = 2 k_{A}=2 augmented images. The original image follows JiT’s preprocessing, a center crop to the training resolution and a random horizontal flip with probability 0.5 0.5 . It is the only input the generative path sees and it is also one contrastive anchor. The two augmented images are used by the representation path alone and follow the SimCLR policy ( Chen et al., 2020a ; Grill et al., 2020 ) : random resized crop with scale in [ 0.08 , 1.0 ] [0.08,1.0] , color jitter of strength ( 0.4 , 0.4 , 0.2 , 0.1 ) (0.4,0.4,0.2,0.1) applied with probability 0.8 0.8 , random grayscale with probability 0.2 0.2 , Gaussian blur with σ \sigma uniform in [ 0.1 , 2.0 ] [0.1,2.0] , and a random horizontal flip. This is what exposes the shared encoder to both regimes every step, noised original images for generation and clean augmented ones for the invariances.

sections.heading: Timestep sampling.
sections.text: For both flow matching losses we sample t t from the logit-normal schedule ( Esser et al., 2024 ) : draw s ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , σ 2 ) s\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) and set t = sigmoid ⁡ ( s ) t=\mathrm{sigmoid}(s) , which we write logit ⁡ ( t ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ , σ 2 ) \operatorname{logit}(t)\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) . The image path uses JiT’s default ( μ , σ ) = ( − 0.8 , 0.8 ) (\mu,\sigma)=(-0.8,0.8) , and the prior path ( μ ′ , σ ′ ) = ( − 1.2 , 0.6 ) (\mu^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})=(-1.2,0.6) , the latter selected on a frozen-prior grid and applied to the RCG baseline as well.

sections.heading: Losses.
sections.text: The contrastive objective is the multi-view form of the Global Contrastive Loss ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) , with fixed temperature τ = 0.15 \tau=0.15 , moving-average parameter γ = 0.9 \gamma=0.9 , and negatives gathered across GPUs. The generative objective is the conditional flow matching loss ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) with 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -prediction and the velocity parameterization of JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) . We clamp the 1 − t 1-t denominator at max ⁡ ( 1 − t , 0.05 ) \max(1-t,0.05) for numerical stability near t = 1 t=1 . The weight λ \lambda on ℒ CL {\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{CL}} comes from the balancer of Section 3.3 and Algorithm 2 : gradient norms are read on the feed-forward submodule of the last encoder block, the estimate is refreshed every 10 10 steps, and the two moving averages use a decay ramped linearly from 0.9 0.9 to 0.99 0.99 over the first 5000 5000 steps. Their ratio is clamped to [ 10 − 3 , 1 ] [10^{-3},1] and multiplied by λ 0 = 1 \lambda_{0}=1 . The CBC weight is fixed at η = 0.01 \eta=0.01 and is not balanced. None of these constants are tuned .

sections.text: At B/16 we train with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) , in bfloat16 mixed precision, under a constant learning rate with a linear warmup over 5 5 epochs and weight decay 0 0 . At L/16 the parameters split across two optimizers: Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) takes the two-dimensional parameters inside the transformer blocks, at learning rate 2 ⋅ 10 − 2 2\cdot 10^{-2} and weight decay 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} , and everything else stays on AdamW at the same learning rate and weight decay as at B/16. Moreover, for L/16, we use a BatchNorm ( Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015 ) after the [CLS] token at the encoder-decoder split. We keep two exponential moving averages of the weights, with decays 0.9999 0.9999 and 0.9996 0.9996 . sections.heading: Checkpoint selection.
sections.text: All metrics are computed on EMA weights. Section 4.1 reports the 400 400 -epoch checkpoint, the budget at which every baseline stops, Section 4.3 reports 200 200 epochs, and Section 4.2 reports SCION (B/16) at 800 800 epochs and SCION (L/16) at 400 400 . We evaluate the EMA with decay 0.9999 0.9999 , except for the system-level comparison, where we evaluate both exponential moving averages and select the 0.9996 0.9996 one only for SCION (L/16).

sections.heading: Generation.
sections.text: All generation numbers use 50 50 K samples drawn with a Heun ODE solver ( Heun, 1900 ) with 50 50 steps (49 Heun steps and a final Euler step). For the class-conditional baselines the batch is 50 50 samples for each of the 1000 1000 ImageNet classes. SCION is class-unconditional and does not use labels for generation either. Instead, we unconditionally sample from the learned prior e ω e_{\omega} the conditioning vectors for the generator. Thus, its batch carries no class structure by construction. Where guidance is reported, it is applied on the interval t ∈ [ 0.1 , 1.0 ] t\in[0.1,1.0] ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) at a scale swept from 1.0 1.0 in steps of 0.1 0.1 on 8000 8000 samples, continuing while FID keeps improving.

sections.heading: Generation metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate generation with the ADM suite ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , using their reference batches and official implementation. 2 2 2 https://github.com/openai/guided-diffusion/tree/main/evaluations All metrics are computed from Inception-V3 outputs on the 50 50 K generated images; all but the Inception Score also read the suite’s ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 reference batch. • FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) is the Fréchet distance between Gaussians fitted to the pooled Inception features of the generated and reference sets. • sFID ( Nash et al., 2021 ) computes the same distance on flattened intermediate spatial features instead of pooled ones, making it more sensitive to errors in spatial structure. • IS ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) is the exponential of the average KL divergence between the class distribution the same Inception-V3 predicts for each generated image and the marginal over all of them. It rises when samples are individually classifiable and collectively spread across classes, and it is the one metric here computed from the generated set alone. • Precision and Recall ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) estimate the support of each distribution with a k k -nearest-neighbor manifold ( k = 3 k=3 ). Precision is the fraction of generated images inside the reference manifold and measures fidelity. Recall is the fraction of reference images inside the generated manifold and measures coverage. Since guidance typically buys fidelity at the cost of coverage, the two should be read together. Not all metrics see the same reference set. FID and sFID are computed against first- and second-moment statistics precomputed over the full reference dataset, while precision and recall are estimated against the 10 ​ K 10K reference images distributed with the batch, not against the full dataset.

sections.heading: Representation.
sections.text: Both probes freeze the network and read one vector per image. For SCION that vector is the [CLS] token at the encoder/decoder split, taken before the contrastive projection head. The baselines carry no [CLS] token, so for them it is the mean of the patch tokens, excluding the in-context conditioning tokens, at their own split. Vanilla JiT and the RCG generator have no split and are read after their last block. The contrastive-only controls carry a [CLS] token and are read like SCION. The ImageNet probe ( Acc. ) fits an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularized multinomial logistic regression on the raw features, with no augmentation: images are resized to 292 292 with bicubic interpolation and center-cropped to 256 256 . The regularization strength is chosen over 45 45 logarithmically spaced values between 10 − 6 10^{-6} and 10 5 10^{5} on a held-out 10 % 10\% of the training split, the classifier is then refit on the full training split at that value, and we report top-1 accuracy on the validation split. The transfer probe ( transfer-8 ) evaluates out-of-domain transfer on Food-101 ( Bossard et al., 2014 ) , CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009 ) , Stanford Cars ( Krause et al., 2013 ) , Describable Textures ( Cimpoi et al., 2014 ) , Oxford-IIIT Pets ( Parkhi et al., 2012 ) , Caltech-101 ( Li et al., 2022 ) and Oxford 102 Flowers ( Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008 ) , and reports their unweighted mean. We follow the evaluation protocol of each dataset’s own paper, so mean per-class accuracy for Caltech-101, Oxford-IIIT Pets and Oxford 102 Flowers and top-1 accuracy for the rest. Features are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized and standardized. We then fit an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularized multinomial logistic regression with the L-BFGS solver of scikit-learn ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ) . Training images are center-cropped to the training resolution of 256 256 with a random horizontal flip, and the flip is removed at test time. We report the best test accuracy over 10 10 logarithmically spaced regularization values between 10 − 3 10^{-3} and 1 1 .

sections.heading: Appendix F Architecture details
sections.text: SCION is a JiT-style pixel-space transformer ( Li and He, 2026 ) with three changes. First, we split the transformer depth into a shared encoder f θ f_{\theta} and a generative decoder g ϕ g_{\phi} , two contiguous portions of one ViT-style backbone ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) with total depth L = L enc + L dec L=L_{\mathrm{enc}}+L_{\mathrm{dec}} . Second, we prepend a learnable [CLS] token and read it out at the encoder/decoder boundary as the global embedding 𝒆 {\bm{e}} . Third, we attach a contrastive projection head h ψ h_{\psi} to that embedding while the patch tokens continue through the decoder for flow matching. Additionally, we condition the generative path on sg ​ ( 𝒆 ) \text{\bf sg}({\bm{e}}) and learn a prior e ω e_{\omega} ( Li et al., 2024a ) over these embeddings for class-unconditional sampling. Table 13 lists each component with its input and output spaces. All remaining architectural choices follow JiT, except for the attention residuals below, which every model we train uses. For completeness, we go into each component in the following paragraphs.

sections.heading: Transformer block.
sections.text: Each block uses pre- RMSNorm ( Zhang and Sennrich, 2019 ) , multi-head self-attention with QK-norm ( Henry et al., 2020 ) and two-dimensional rotary positional embeddings ( Su et al., 2024 ) , then a second pre- RMSNorm and a SwiGLU feed-forward network ( Shazeer, 2020 ) whose inner width is 8 3 ​ d \tfrac{8}{3}d , an MLP ratio of 4 4 under SwiGLU ’s two-thirds rescaling. As in DiT and JiT, both residual branches are modulated by adaLN-Zero ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) : a linear projection of the conditioning vector produces shift, scale and gate parameters for the two sublayers, and the modulation layers are zero-initialized so each branch begins near the identity.

sections.heading: Attention residuals.
sections.text: Applied to every model we train in Section 4 , ours and all baselines, attention residuals ( Kimi Team et al., 2026 ) replace the plain residual add of each sublayer. The sublayers stay pre-norm, since what changes is the residual stream and not where the normalization sits. Instead of reading the running residual sum, a sublayer reads a learned softmax-weighted mixture over its depth history and appends its own output to that history: the keys are the normalized history entries, and the query is a learned vector per token role (patch, [CLS] or in-context tokens). Writing 𝒔 1 , … , 𝒔 n ∈ ℝ d {\bm{s}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for the entries at one token position of role ρ \rho , that mixture is 𝒔 ^ = ∑ i = 1 n α i ​ 𝒔 i , α i = exp ⁡ ⟨ 𝒒 ρ , RMSNorm ⁡ ( 𝒔 i ) ⟩ ∑ l = 1 n exp ⁡ ⟨ 𝒒 ρ , RMSNorm ⁡ ( 𝒔 l ) ⟩ , \hat{{\bm{s}}}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\,{\bm{s}}_{i},\qquad\alpha_{i}\;=\;\frac{\exp\big\langle{\bm{q}}_{\rho},\,\mathrm{RMSNorm}({\bm{s}}_{i})\big\rangle}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\exp\big\langle{\bm{q}}_{\rho},\,\mathrm{RMSNorm}({\bm{s}}_{l})\big\rangle}, (22) a softmax over depth with no 1 / d 1/\sqrt{d} scaling. A history entry is the sum of four consecutive sublayer outputs, which bounds the number of entries the mixture runs over. The queries are zero-initialized, so the mixture is uniform at initialization.

sections.heading: Patch and positional embeddings.
sections.text: Images are tokenized by a low-rank linear patch embedder ( Li and He, 2026 ) : a p × p p\times p strided convolution maps non-overlapping RGB patches into a bottleneck of width 128 128 , followed by a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution to the transformer width d d . Two positional signals are used and they act at different places. Fixed two-dimensional sine-cosine embeddings ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) are added to the patch tokens only, before the [CLS] and in-context tokens are concatenated. The rotary embeddings act inside attention, on the queries and keys after QK-norm, with an identity rotation at the non-patch positions so that the [CLS] and in-context tokens carry no spatial position. The final layer applies RMSNorm , adaLN modulation and a zero-initialized linear projection to p 2 ​ c out p^{2}c_{\mathrm{out}} values per patch, which are unpatchified into an image.

sections.heading: Conditioning.
sections.text: The timestep is embedded with sinusoidal features followed by a two-layer SiLU ( Elfwing et al., 2018 ) MLP. The conditioning vector 𝒄 {\bm{c}} passes through a linear projection and then enters the network twice. It is added to the timestep embedding that drives the adaLN-Zero modulation of every block, and the same projected vector is also injected as 32 32 in-context tokens at a fixed block, following the design of JiT and MAR ( Li and He, 2026 ; Li et al., 2024b ) . These tokens are added on the fourth block for B/16 and the eighth for L/16. The in-context tokens are removed before the final image projection. On the representation pass the conditioning input is the learned null 𝒆 ∅ {\bm{e}}_{\varnothing} , and classifier-free guidance uses a second learned null 𝒄 ∅ {\bm{c}}_{\varnothing} .

sections.heading: Encoder/decoder split.
sections.text: At block L enc L_{\mathrm{enc}} the [CLS] token is read out as the global embedding. At B/16 the readout is the raw token; at L/16 it passes through a BatchNorm ( Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015 ) . The [CLS] token is dropped at the split and never reaches the decoder, so the decoder is a function of the patch tokens 𝒉 {\bm{h}} alone. Our SCION (B/16) splits ( L enc , L dec ) = ( 8 , 4 ) (L_{\mathrm{enc}},L_{\mathrm{dec}})=(8,4) of 12 12 blocks at width 768 768 with 12 12 heads, and SCION (L/16) splits ( 16 , 8 ) (16,8) of 24 24 at width 1024 1024 with 16 16 heads.

sections.heading: Contrastive head.
sections.text: The projection head h ψ h_{\psi} is a two-hidden-layer MLP, d → 2048 → 2048 → 256 d\to 2048\to 2048\to 256 , followed by ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalization. It is used by ℒ CL {\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{CL}} and by nothing else, so it is discarded after training.

sections.heading: Prior.
sections.text: It is a residual MLP over a single vector with additive timestep conditioning. That is, a linear layer maps the noised embedding 𝒆 ~ t ′ ∈ ℝ d \widetilde{{\bm{e}}}_{t^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to width C C . The timestep is encoded with 256 256 sinusoidal features and a two-layer SiLU MLP to width C C . The hidden vector then passes through N N residual blocks, each applying RMSNorm , a SwiGLU projection to the block width, an additive linear projection of the timestep embedding, and a linear projection back to C C . A final RMSNorm , SiLU and linear layer return to ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} . Every block’s output projection and the final projection are zero-initialized, so each block is the identity and the prior predicts zero at initialization. The prior uses additive residual connections and it is trained with the same 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -prediction flow matching parameterization as the image path, in representation space. sections.heading: Appendix G Qualitative results using learned representations
sections.text: SCION extracts its own semantic representations and uses them to condition generation. We explore this connection through qualitative experiments using representations produced by the model itself. First, we generate from real-image representations to examine whether the outputs preserve the references’ semantic content. We then interpolate between two image representations to explore how the generated content changes along the resulting path. All examples use SCION (L/16) at 400 400 epochs. Generated images use representation guidance with a scaling factor s = 2.0 s=2.0 (see Equation 6 ). Reference images come from the ImageNet training set, except flower buds in Figure 6 which are external photographs. Real references show the same 256 × 256 256\times 256 crops supplied to the encoder. This section is meant to illustrate qualitative behavior rather than quantify reconstruction accuracy or diversity.

sections.heading: G.1 Generation from real-image representations
sections.text: We encode each reference image and directly supply its representation to the generator, bypassing the prior. The pairs in Figure 4 illustrate preservation of semantic content without exact reproduction of image details. Generated images retain recognizable subjects and scene types, while pose, color, object markings, backgrounds, and architectural details can change. For example, a cup retains its identity as a cup while its decoration changes, and a building remains recognizable as the same type of structure despite changes in its facade. Thus, the model’s own representations support semantically related generation without requiring the output to reconstruct the particular reference image.

sections.heading: G.2 Interpolation between image representations
sections.text: We next interpolate between the representations of two real images and generate from the intermediate vectors (Figures 5 and 6 ). We use spherical interpolation of their directions and linear interpolation of their magnitudes in the generator’s conditioning space, bypassing the prior. Image-sampling noise is held fixed within each row, so changes along a path reflect changes in the conditioning representation. In Figure 5 , the paths first explore appearance and scene composition within a class, then connect different classes, from two dog breeds to more distant concepts such as a bottle and a dog. These cross-class paths reveal how structures from the endpoints can blend, although their intermediate images need not depict plausible natural objects. Figure 6 applies the same interpolation mechanism to five selected pairs of bud and open-flower representations. Bud photographs were obtained externally and were not part of the training set. Open-flower photographs come from the ImageNet training set and were manually matched to the buds. Thus, the paired photographs may depict different individual flowers. These are representation interpolations, not observed growth sequences or predictions of a particular bud’s future appearance. The selected paths show opening-like changes in flower structure, while endpoint color and details can drift. The six generated images include endpoint reconstructions at α = 0 \alpha=0 and 1 1 ; these are distinct from the real photographs. While effective, the cost is that generation becomes contingent on supervision and pretraining: labels must be annotated, and encoders, autoencoders, and tokenizers must be pretrained for the target domain. This paper studies joint generative and self-supervised representation learning in one model , such that generation is self-conditioned without any labels or pretrained models. This is challenging since the two objectives are mismatched: contrastive learning consumes clean augmented views and keeps coarse, invariant semantics, while flow matching consumes noisy images and must preserve the fine detail and spatial layout that contrastive learning discards. We propose a framework Self-conditioned Generation on Self-supervised representation (SCION), whose core is a single pixel-space encoder conditioned on both the diffusion timestep and a conditioning embedding. The encoder serves two roles that differ in what that embedding is. For representation learning, the conditioning embedding is one learned global vector shared by all images, and the encoder’s [CLS] token yields the semantic embedding trained by the contrastive loss. For generative training, the conditioning embedding is the [CLS] embedding of the image itself, and the encoder’s patch tokens pass through a decoder to predict the image. To sample without a reference image at inference, we also learn a prior over the embedding in the same run. With gradient-norm balancing and stop-gradient tricks, all losses are jointly optimized in a single run. The resulting method is fully self-supervised, with no pretrained model and no labels. On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , with the same JiT-B/16 recipe and without representation guidance, SCION reaches 8.92 8.92 FID, surpassing the class-unconditional baselines iREPA, which aligns to a pretrained DINOv2 ( 46.44 46.44 ), and RCG, which conditions on it ( 14.27 14.27 ). Under the JiT-L/16 recipe, SCION achieves the best pixel-space class-unconditional FID of 5.89 5.89 and 3.47 3.47 without and with representation guidance, outperforming RCG with the ADM recipe ( 6.24 6.24 ). 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in image generation ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Yet many strong systems rely on class labels for semantic conditioning ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Li and He, 2026 ) , frozen pretrained encoders for conditioning or representation alignment ( Li et al., 2024a ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) , or separately trained autoencoders for latent-space generation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . These dependencies add annotation or pretraining costs and complicate extension to domains where suitable labels or pretrained models are unavailable. A central challenge is therefore to enable semantically self-conditioned generation , where the semantic representations that condition generation are learned within the diffusion model itself, jointly with the generative process. We pursue semantic self-conditioned generation under four “S” requirements: self-contained , without pretrained components, including autoencoders and tokenizers; self-supervised , without label supervision anywhere in the pipeline, including that inherited through pretrained components; single-model , with representations produced by the generator’s own network; and single-stage , with all components learned jointly from scratch. Existing methods (cf. Table 1 ) address different aspects of this goal but satisfy these requirements only partially ( Li and He, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2023 ; Preechakul et al., 2022 ; Hudson et al., 2024 ; Wang and He, 2025 ) . These comparisons highlight the remaining challenge: achieving semantic self-conditioning under all four “S” requirements, with useful representations and unconditional synthesis learned together within one model. A natural approach to semantically self-conditioned generation is to learn the conditioning representations through contrastive self-supervised learning, which extracts semantics directly from unlabeled images ( Chen et al., 2020a ; He et al., 2020 ; Yuan et al., 2022 ) . However, integrating self-supervised representation learning with flow matching in one network requires reconciling their conflicting input and output requirements. Contrastive learning operates on clean augmented views and encourages compact semantic embeddings that suppress variations in appearance and spatial layout. Flow matching instead operates on noisy images and requires dense predictions that recover fine visual detail and spatial structure. The shared network must therefore accommodate both clean and noisy inputs while supporting semantic invariance without discarding information needed for synthesis. Joint training further couples the generator to an evolving conditioning representation, and sampling requires obtaining conditioning embeddings without a reference image. To address these challenges, we propose S elf- C onditioned Generation on Self-Supervised Representat ion (SCION), a framework for semantically self-conditioned generation through joint generative and self-supervised representation learning. At its core is a single pixel-space transformer encoder conditioned on both a timestep and a conditioning embedding. Our key idea is to use this encoder in two conditioning modes with different readouts. For representation learning, the encoder processes clean augmented views using a learned global conditioning vector shared across all images, and a contrastive objective trains its [CLS] embedding. For generative learning, the same encoder processes noisy images conditioned on the clean image’s own [CLS] embedding, and a decoder maps its patch tokens to a clean-image prediction under a flow matching objective. This design keeps contrastive inputs clean while using spatial features for generation, allowing both objectives to train the shared encoder. To coordinate joint optimization, we employ gradient-norm balancing and stop-gradient operations. We also train a prior over the learned embeddings in the same run, enabling generation without reference images. Randomly withholding the conditioning embedding during training also supports classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) , with guidance supplied by learned representations rather than class labels. All components are trained jointly from scratch, without labels, pretrained teachers, latent autoencoders, or tokenizers. We evaluate on ImageNet at 256 × 256 256\times 256 against flow-based baselines matched on the JiT-B/16 recipe. SCION reaches 8.92 8.92 FID, improving by 6.1 × 6.1\times over the strongest self-contained baseline ( 54.14 54.14 ), and outperforming methods that import pretrained semantics, either aligning with them (iREPA, 46.44 46.44 ) or conditioning on them (RCG at matched training budget, 14.27 14.27 ). Self-representation guidance further reduces SCION to 4.20 4.20 FID, outperforming representation-guided RCG ( 5.01 5.01 ) without importing a pretrained encoder. At larger scale, SCION (JiT-L/16) reaches 5.89 5.89 unguided FID, improving on the 6.24 6.24 reported by pixel-space RCG with an ADM training recipe. We first conduct a controlled comparison with baselines that share the same backbone, training budget, and flow-matching recipe, isolating the contribution of the proposed framework. We then compare with published unconditional pixel-space systems using their reported scores, providing a system-level reference. Finally, we ablate SCION to identify the contribution of each component and compare its representation with that of a contrastive-only model. Baselines . We compare SCION with vanilla flow matching (FM) and four methods built on it: Dispersive Loss ( Wang and He, 2025 ) , REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , iREPA ( Singh et al., 2026 ) , and RCG ( Li et al., 2024a ) . Thus, the baselines span FM alone, self-contained feature regularization (Dispersive), external-feature alignment (REPA/iREPA), and external semantic conditioning (RCG). Setup . All controlled methods use the same JiT-B/16 backbone ( Li and He, 2026 ) with attention residuals (Appendix F ), flow matching recipe, ImageNet-1K ( 256 × 256 256\times 256 ) training data ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) , and a total training budget of 400 400 epochs. The baselines that import semantics use a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , pretrained on external data. REPA and iREPA retain their original split of 4 4 encoder and 8 8 decoder blocks, whereas Dispersive Loss and SCION use 8 8 encoder and 4 4 decoder blocks. We split RCG’s training budget between its generator and prior, training for 200 200 epochs each. We also evaluate RCG with both its original prior architecture and ours: the original architecture performs better, so we report that result. Evaluation . We evaluate generation with FID and Inception Score (IS) under the ADM protocol ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) on 50 50 K samples. We evaluate representations using ImageNet top-1 accuracy ( Acc. ) and the average accuracy across eight datasets for transfer learning ( transfer-8 ; datasets listed in Appendix E.2 ). For both probes, we train a logistic-regression classifier on the frozen representations produced by the model. For the baselines, the representation is the mean pooling of patch token embeddings at the encoder–decoder split, or after the last block for vanilla JiT and RCG; for SCION, we use its [CLS] token at its own split.
